title_en: From Accountant to Ice Cream Founder: Lessons from Little Moons
title_zh: 从会计师到冰淇淋创始人：Little Moons 的创业启示
summary_zh: 维维安·黄（Vivien Wong）辞去年薪8万英镑的会计工作，与哥哥霍华德共同创立麻糬冰淇淋品牌 Little Moons。该品牌在 TikTok 上爆红，但实际经历了十多年的积累。她分享了产品不必追求完美、坚持品牌定位、谨慎对待专家建议以及家人共事需设定边界等创业经验，并强调一夜成名往往建立在长期准备之上。
reading_passage:
Vivien Wong founded mochi brand Little Moons with her brother Howard

At 28, Vivien Wong walked away from an £80,000-a-year accounting job to start making ice cream with her brother.

Growing up in her family's bakery, she had dreamt of one day running her own business. She says her father's cancer diagnosis made her take the leap to create Little Moons.

The mochi balls of doughy rice filled with ice-cream exploded on TikTok, but its apparent overnight success was more than a decade in the making.

Wong shares the lessons she learnt along the way and her advice for anyone thinking about starting a business of their own.

Little Moons co-founder Vivien Wong: Your product doesn't have to be perfect

One of the biggest mistakes aspiring founders make is waiting for everything to be perfect so Wong recommends following an "80-20 rule".

"Don't wait for perfection because that extra 20 is going to take you too long and you might miss the market," she says.

Instead, she recommends getting a product "80% of the way there", launching it and improving it as you go - like she did with Little Moons.

For its first five years Wong sold mochi to restaurants and cinemas before she saved enough money to invest in branding and move into supermarkets.

Wong left a well-paid job and moved in with her brother so they could save money and reinvest any profits into the business.

She remembers swapping a polished City environment, where there was always someone else to call for help, for having to do almost everything herself.

"All roads lead to you when you run your own business so even though I wasn't great with IT, I was head of IT".

She also had to learn about machinery, product development, making ice cream and paying wages.

Wong says she even did the company accounts on Sundays rather than pay for a bookkeeper because, at the time, saving the money mattered more than getting the day back.

Wong's advice to people starting a business is about the importance of knowing your brand and saying no to opportunities that don't fit.

"If you know what your brand values are, you know how you can apply that to a trend, but you also know when to leave it alone," she says.

"Pick and choose what you say yes to and don't try and do everything. Stay focused, know exactly what you stand for."

She also warns against blindly taking advice from experts - but to listen and think for yourself.

"You realise that advice they're giving you was probably right for another business but not for your specific set of circumstances."

She and her brother would discuss advice they received, sometimes take it and sometimes reject it and over time, making those decisions helped build her confidence.

Vivien says she and brother Howard had to see one another as colleagues rather than siblings while they built their company

Wong says working with her brother has been a huge strength but there were also "definitely a lot of arguments".

They had to learn to behave like colleagues at work rather than siblings.

When the company was considering moving from a 5,000 sq ft factory to a 30,000 sq ft site, with annual rent jumping from around £40,000 to £500,000, Wong says she was more willing to take the risk while her brother was naturally more cautious.

But that difference in opinion has helped them make better decisions as they "balance each other out".

Her advice for anyone working with family is to set boundaries for how you interact in the workplace.

"You have to be really mindful that you're being as respectful to your brother as a colleague and you see him as a colleague and not a sibling," she says.

Now that Little Moons has a chief executive and wider leadership team, the pair are less involved in the day-to-day running of the company which Wong says has allowed them to "just be brother and sister again".

Little Moons became a TikTok phenomenon during the pandemic but Wong says most people don't realise it had been running for a decade already.

"Everyone says we're like an overnight success 12 years in the making," she says.

Before going viral, the company had spent years learning how to manufacture at scale, train staff, export products and supply major retailers.

That preparation proved essential when demand suddenly exploded as the business might not have survived its viral moment without the team and infrastructure already behind it.

"Business is a combination of many, many, many boring things and many boring small steps," she says.

For anyone watching founders seemingly blow up on social media overnight, she says it's important to remember that the viral moment is often the part of the story everyone sees rather than the beginning.

vocabulary.example: Many founders underestimate the time needed to build a customer base.

vocabulary.meaning_zh: 再投资；把（利润）重新投入
vocabulary.example: The company decided to reinvest its annual profits into research and development.
A clear brand identity helps customers understand what a business stands for.

vocabulary.meaning_zh: 界限；边界（此处指工作中与家人相处的规则）
vocabulary.example: The manager set clear boundaries between her personal and professional life.

vocabulary.meaning_zh: 一夜成名的现象；看似突然的成功
collocations: appear to be an overnight success
vocabulary.example: The app became an overnight success, but the developers had worked on it for five years.

vocabulary.meaning_zh: 日常运营；日常工作管理
collocations: be involved in the day-to-day running
vocabulary.example: She handed over the day-to-day running of the shop to her manager.

vocabulary.meaning_zh: 二八法则；80/20 规则（指不需要追求完美，做到八成即可）
vocabulary.example: The team applied the 80-20 rule to launch the product before all features were complete.
She walked away from a senior role to start her own consultancy.

vocabulary.meaning_zh: 迅速走红；爆发式增长（在社交媒体上）
vocabulary.example: The singer blew up on TikTok after her video was shared by a celebrity.

vocabulary.meaning_zh: 基础设施；基础架构（此处指支撑企业运营的团队、系统和流程）
vocabulary.example: The company invested heavily in its logistics infrastructure before expanding internationally.

difficult_sentences.sentence: The mochi balls of doughy rice filled with ice-cream exploded on TikTok, but its apparent overnight success was more than a decade in the making.
difficult_sentences.explanation_zh: 主句为 “The mochi balls ... exploded on TikTok”，后接由 but 连接的并列句 “its apparent overnight success was more than a decade in the making”。句中 “filled with ice-cream” 是过去分词短语作后置定语，修饰 “balls of doughy rice”；“apparent” 暗示这种成功看似突然，与后文 “more than a decade” 形成对比。
difficult_sentences.grammar_point: 过去分词短语作后置定语；并列转折结构。
difficult_sentences.translation_zh: 这种糯米团冰淇淋在 TikTok 上爆红，但它看似一夜成名实际上酝酿了十多年。

difficult_sentences.sentence: She remembers swapping a polished City environment, where there was always someone else to call for help, for having to do almost everything herself.
difficult_sentences.explanation_zh: 主句是 “She remembers swapping ... for having ...”。动名词短语 “swapping A for B” 表示用 A 换取 B；“a polished City environment” 后接 where 引导的定语从句，补充说明在大公司有人可求助；“having to do almost everything herself” 是动名词短语，作 for 的宾语。
difficult_sentences.grammar_point: 动名词短语作 remember 的宾语；where 引导非限制性定语从句；swap A for B 结构。
difficult_sentences.translation_zh: 她回忆说，自己告别了光鲜的金融城环境——在那里总有人可以求助——转而几乎事事都要亲力亲为。

difficult_sentences.sentence: When the company was considering moving from a 5,000 sq ft factory to a 30,000 sq ft site, with annual rent jumping from around £40,000 to £500,000, Wong says she was more willing to take the risk while her brother was naturally more cautious.
difficult_sentences.explanation_zh: 句子以 When 引导的时间状语从句开头，说明背景；主句是 “Wong says...”，后接省略 that 的宾语从句 “she was more willing...”。宾语从句中含有 while 引导的对比状语从句，突出两人态度差异；“with annual rent jumping from...to...” 是 with 复合结构作伴随状语，补充说明搬迁成本。
difficult_sentences.grammar_point: When 时间状语从句；with 复合结构作伴随状语；while 表示对比；宾语从句省略 that。
difficult_sentences.translation_zh: 当公司考虑从 5000 平方英尺的工厂搬到 30000 平方英尺的场地、年租金从约 4 万英镑涨到 50 万英镑时，Wong 说她更愿意冒险，而她哥哥天生更谨慎。

difficult_sentences.sentence: That preparation proved essential when demand suddenly exploded as the business might not have survived its viral moment without the team and infrastructure already behind it.
difficult_sentences.explanation_zh: 主句是 “That preparation proved essential”，后接 when 引导的时间状语从句；“as the business might not have survived...” 是原因状语从句，说明 preparation 为什么至关重要；其中 “without the team and infrastructure already behind it” 是介词短语作条件状语，使用虚拟语气 “might not have survived” 表示与过去事实相反的假设。
difficult_sentences.grammar_point: when 时间状语从句；as 原因状语从句；without 介词短语表虚拟条件；情态动词 might have done 表示对过去的推测。
difficult_sentences.translation_zh: 当需求突然爆发时，这种准备就显得至关重要，因为如果没有背后已有的团队和基础设施，公司可能无法挺过那个病毒式传播的时刻。

idioms.meaning_zh: 大胆尝试；冒险迈出关键一步
idioms.usage_note: 口语化表达，常用于描述放弃稳定状态、开始新事业或做出重大决定。可单独使用，也可接“and do something”。
idioms.example: After years of planning, she finally took the leap and opened her own bakery.

idioms.meaning_zh: 所有事情最终都要由你负责（此处化用谚语 all roads lead to Rome，强调创业者必须亲自处理各种事务）
idioms.usage_note: 非固定习语，是说话人对常见谚语的创造性使用；在商业语境中表示责任集中。仅在类似创业、领导场景中使用，不宜用于描述客观交通。
idioms.example: When you start a company, all roads lead to you, so you must be ready to handle everything from IT to accounting.

idioms.meaning_zh: 互相平衡；互补抵消（指双方不同的特点共同形成更稳妥的决策）
idioms.usage_note: 常用于描述两人或两组人性格、观点互补，使结果更合理。通常接“each other”或“one another”。
idioms.example: Her optimism and his caution balance each other out, which makes them a strong management team.

idioms.meaning_zh: 仔细挑选；有选择地接受
idioms.usage_note: 非正式表达，强调有标准地筛选，而不是全盘接受。常与“what to do”“which opportunities to take”等搭配。
idioms.example: As a freelancer, you can pick and choose which projects align with your values.

reading_questions.question: What is the main idea of the passage?

options.A: Little Moons became successful only because of TikTok.
options.B: Vivien Wong's journey shows that persistence, brand focus, and preparation matter more than overnight success.
options.C: Working with family members is the biggest obstacle for entrepreneurs.
options.D: Leaving a well-paid job guarantees business success.

reading_questions.question: Who founded Little Moons according to the passage?

options.C: Vivien Wong and her brother Howard.

reading_questions.question: What can be inferred about Wong's decision to create Little Moons?

options.A: It was mainly a way to avoid working as an accountant.
options.B: She expected the product to become a TikTok trend.
options.C: It was influenced by both a personal dream and a family health crisis.
options.D: She was following advice from business experts.

reading_questions.question: In paragraph 4, the word "exploded" is closest in meaning to:
What is the author's attitude toward Wong's move from a high-paying job to ice cream making?
What is the function of the concluding paragraph in the passage?

options.A: It introduces a new example of a startup failure.
options.B: It reinforces the idea that viral success is usually the result of long preparation.
options.C: It provides detailed financial data to support the argument.
options.D: It shifts focus to the role of social media in modern business.

reading_questions.question: Which of the following would be the best title for the passage?

options.A: From Accountant to Ice Cream Maker: The Lessons Behind Little Moons
options.B: The Rise and Fall of a TikTok Food Trend
options.C: How to Earn £80,000 a Year in Accounting

sources.title: I quit my £80,000 job to make ice cream - here's how
